analysis.title: Monthly CIO View – Private Banking (13 November 2026): Does the recent volatility in the tech sector herald the bursting of the AI bubble?
key_insights: October saw a sharp sector rotation out of technology. Most MSCI World sectors rose, but tech declines weighed on the index. The median S&P 500 stock gained 10.3% while the index fell 0.9%, held back by its six largest constituents (down 7.1% on average). The equal-weighted S&P 500 rose 4.9% and the SOX fell 15.4%, a 25% decline since end of June.

Since the 10-year UST yield peaked on October 5, the best S&P 500 sectors have been defensives: consumer staples, healthcare and utilities. Sovereign yields fell from their September highs despite stronger-than-expected growth.
Risk reduction was global. Euro Stoxx 50 outperformed on lower tech exposure (Stoxx 600 +1.9%, banks -9.9% as yields rose). Swiss SPI +6.3% on pharma. Nikkei 225 -5.2% in JPY. Korean Kospi -16.2%.

AI valuations compressed sharply. Semiconductor P/E fell from 29x at the June 15 peak to 14x in early November. Nasdaq 100 fell from nearly 23x at end-September to 18x in early November. Hyperscalers underperformed the S&P 500 by an average of 26% over the month.

After Democrats took both houses of Congress in the midterms, markets first rose and oil fell. The move reversed on 5 November on fears of slower US data-centre buildout. The sell-off hit semiconductors, AI-exposed industrials, servers and neoclouds, then spread more mildly to the broader market.

The speed and size of the 5 November correction point to heavy leverage and forced liquidations by some hedge funds. Rising tech correlations, weak momentum strategies and unwinding factor exposures are consistent with broad short-term de-risking.

Risk of another short-term correction remains significant. Residual hedge fund leverage is hard to measure, and volatility, funding constraints and political uncertainty argue for caution. Stable funding markets, normalised hyperscaler cash flows and key technical levels will be decisive.

Historical base rate: only about 40 daily Nasdaq declines of more than 5% in 25 years. Three months later the Nasdaq averaged +4% with a 55% hit ratio, and 100% hit ratio with a 19% average return since 2010.

The one-month performance gap between the equal-weighted S&P and the Magnificent Seven is near its all-time high of almost 12%, which historically signals a reversal. US low-quality credit spreads are still low at 340bps, and recent big-tech bond issues drew record demand.

The bank argues the market is too alarmist on the political risk. Democrat control raises the chance of tighter regulation delaying data centre projects, especially in Texas (expected 25-30% of construction by 2030). The bank sees at most a slowdown, with protests aimed at local deployment without safeguards, not AI itself.

The bank's models say first-tier AI names (chips, optics, hyperscalers) price in a 30-80% cut to capex by 2030, and second-tier names (equipment, data centre infrastructure) a 15-30% decline. Consensus hyperscaler capex for the five majors is $379B in 2025, $847B in 2026 and $1,345B in 2030. Even a 30% cut would leave capex 2.5x the 2025 level.

Other drivers of volatility: the Nvidia CEO resigned after revelations about extra-marital affairs, and CPI and PPI came in above forecasts, lifting US rate expectations for next month. CoreWeave's reassuring results eased neocloud financing fears and the Nasdaq recovered almost all of the 5 November decline within days.

Central scenario: equity volatility stays high, driven more by technical than fundamental factors. Higher-quality tech with strong balance sheets and revenue visibility could offer entry points. Names dependent on external financing and continued infrastructure acceleration carry higher risk. Earnings are mostly above expectations. Central banks face decisions in coming weeks and may be influenced by the Iran-US peace talks via oil prices and inflation expectations.

sector_views.rationale: Valuations price in deep capex cuts and the sell-off is seen as technical, so quality names with revenue visibility could offer attractive entry points.
Names reliant on abundant external financing and continued acceleration in infrastructure spending carry a higher risk profile.
They led since October 5, but the report only describes the move and gives no forward stance.

earnings_insights: Corporate earnings published so far are generally above analysts' expectations and should bring more visibility to the market.
CoreWeave's results were described as reassuring and eased fears about the financing of highly leveraged neoclouds (no figures given).

macro_indicators.interpretation: The hot print raised expectations of a US rate hike next month and weighed on markets.
Together with CPI it raised US rate expectations and weighed on markets.

macro_indicators.reading: Peaked October 5, then fell (no level given)
macro_indicators.interpretation: Yields fell from September highs as investors de-risked into defensives.
Spreads remain low, so there is no broad credit sell-off despite the tech correction.

risk_factors: Further hedge fund deleveraging and forced liquidations.
Political and regulatory delays to US data centre projects, notably in Texas.
Higher US rate expectations after hot CPI and PPI prints.
Leveraged, externally financed AI players such as neoclouds.
Oil prices and inflation expectations tied to the Iran-US peace talks.
vol_and_positioning: Equity volatility is expected to stay high, driven more by technical than fundamental factors.

The 5 November sell-off suggests a significant build-up of leverage and forced hedge fund liquidations. Tech correlations rose, momentum strategies underperformed and risk-factor exposures were unwound.
Residual hedge fund leverage is difficult to measure, and the risk of further deleveraging remains substantial.
The one-month gap between the equal-weighted S&P 500 and the Magnificent Seven is near its record of almost 12%, which historically precedes a reversal.
geopolitical: Iran-US peace talks and their effect on oil prices and inflation expectations may influence central bank decisions in the coming weeks.
US midterm elections: Democrats took control of both houses of Congress, raising fears of tighter regulation and delays to US data centre projects, especially in Texas.

tension_points.bull_case: Valuations already price in a 30-80% capex cut for first-tier AI names. Even with a 30% cut, hyperscaler capex would be 2.5x the 2025 level. Nasdaq has historically rebounded after 5% down days, the equal-weight/Mag 7 gap near 12% signals reversal, and credit spreads and big-tech bond demand are strong.
tension_points.bear_case: Residual hedge fund leverage is hard to measure, funding constraints and political uncertainty remain, and Democratic control could delay data centre projects. Hot CPI and PPI prints raised US rate hike expectations.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Failure of funding markets to stabilise, hyperscaler cash flows failing to normalise, or loss of key technical levels.

theme_stances.key_argument: The market is pricing very unfavourable scenarios for AI capex, and a slowdown would not break the structural trend.
theme_stances.evidence: the market is adopting an overly alarmist reading of events

theme_stances.key_argument: The 5 November speed and size of the drop point to forced liquidations, and further deleveraging risk remains substantial.
theme_stances.evidence: the risk of further deleveraging by hedge funds remains substantial
